cues.text: According to an account first written down in 1216, two millers in the Bavarian village of Benningen had carried on a bitter feud for years.

Tradition holds that one of them, exasperated after yet another argument, received Holy Communion and afterward concealed the consecrated host among the stones of his rival's mill, intending to have his neighbor discovered and accused of sacrilege in his place.
The plan, tradition relates, did not unfold as its author intended.
The hidden host is said to have begun to bleed, drawing attention to the very place where it lay hidden.
This exposed the guilt of the man who had planted it rather than the innocent miller he had hoped to frame.
Confronted with what had occurred, the guilty miller repented and confessed his deception.
Word of the sign reached the Bishop of Augsburg, Frederich, who is said to have deposited the recovered host in the Church of St. Martin in nearby Memmingen.

By 1221 the people of Benningen had begun building a chapel on the site of the miracle, known ever since as the Riedkapelle zum Hochwürdigen Gut, later enlarged between 1674 and 1718 to accommodate growing numbers of pilgrims.

Over the centuries that followed, the relic itself was lost track of amid the disruptions of history, though the chapel's original devotional paintings, long mistaken for later copies, were confirmed authentic during a restoration in 1987.
Each year on the Feast of Corpus Christi, the parish of Benningen still processes to the Riedkapelle.
There, it commemorates a sign whose physical trace was lost long ago.
Yet it drew a whole community’s memory around a single truth: malice aimed at a neighbor found itself, in the account tradition preserves, turned back upon the one who intended it.

We recognize in this quiet Bavarian tradition something worth carrying forward even eight centuries later — that reconciliation, however it comes, is never beneath God's notice, even when it arrives through the unraveling of an old and bitter grudge.
